#8423. Buy Medigap in Your Six-Month Window – Don’t Count on Fall Open Enrollment

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Apply for a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) policy in the six months that start once you’re 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. In that one-time window, insurers can’t turn you down or charge more because of your health. In most states, Medicare’s fall open enrollment offers no second chance, so don’t wait for it.

Once your six months end, insurers can ask about your health, then turn you down or charge more, unless a guaranteed-issue right applies. Major insurers’ applications list even high blood pressure as possible grounds for denial, a KFF review found. Only Connecticut and New York give everyone 65 and older another chance year-round. Massachusetts guarantees one every February and March, and Maine once a year for Plan A.

Two different periods are called open enrollment. Your six months are the Medigap Open Enrollment Period. Medicare’s fall open enrollment, Oct. 15 to Dec. 7, is for joining, switching, or dropping Medicare Advantage and drug plans, and only Rhode Island and Minnesota tie limited Medigap windows to it. State birthday rules don’t help first-time buyers either, since they only let people who already have Medigap switch plans.

If you work past 65, the window opens when Part B starts, even while you have a job-based plan, and can close before you need Medigap. When that plan pays before Medicare, as it does at employers with 20 or more workers, you can delay Part B without a late penalty and save the window for when the coverage ends. Helping a parent? Their Medicare card lists the Part B start date under MEDICAL.

Losing a Medicare Advantage plan brings a separate right, covered in our guide to Medigap after an Advantage plan ends.

Mutual of Omaha is a strong place to apply. Mutual of Omaha Insurance Company holds an A+ (Superior) financial strength rating from AM Best. Its online tool prices Plan G from your ZIP code, birth date, and sex, no contact details needed, and you can apply online. Couples can save with its household discount where it’s available, though the amount and rules vary by state.

Our Mutual of Omaha review has sample quotes from three cities. Plan G benefits don’t vary by insurer, so compare your quote with Medicare.gov’s Plan G prices for your ZIP code, then apply while your window is open.

#8422. Everest West Ridge Thwarts Climbers a Second Time

The three-man Russian team returned to Everest’s West Ridge but found the route even more difficult than they expected. After two days of struggle, they’re heading back to Base Camp.

On October 20, Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov went back up to the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide plateau beyond. They still had time to fix more rope higher up.

“We moved…over terrain we’d already covered on the previous rotation,” the climbers texted to team member Natalya Belyankina, who had to abandon the expedition due to illness.

“The weather is good: sunny, with light winds, but cold,” they noted. “Progress was painfully slow today due to heavy packs and a persistent cough,” the climbers noted later.

On Wednesday, they hoped to reach 7,500m, spend the night there, check the route ahead, and then retreat to the plateau. However, they didn’t get as far as they had planned.

“We didn’t cover much ground today,” leader Andrei Vsiliev texted Anna Piunova of The Mountain Club. “The route is no walk in the park. We have to climb steep snowy slopes that conceal rock sections underneath.”

To make things worse, they found no suitable bivy spots at their highest point, so they had to retreat to a place where they could pitch their tent for the night. Today, they were just too exhausted to keep going.

“We’re heading down; we’re sick and need to recover,” Vasiliev told Belyankina. “We can barely keep moving.”

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8421. The Shockingly Simple Math Behind Social Security

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who currently draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

Those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

That little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:

If you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

In between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

First let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:

When you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:

At that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be big enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re new to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

What this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:

Whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result!  Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

To really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a big lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:

So the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

And of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

The net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:

Can we just put this in ONE SIMPLE TABLE based on some reasonable assumptions?

Yes, absolutely! Just to hit the most common situation, let’s assume a household that has

How much is this future benefit worth you you, based on your current age?

These aren’t enormous FAT Fire numbers, but every one of them is enough to feel like a meaningful contribution to your eventual early jump into freedom. For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a big boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

Sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all issues. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Log yourself into ssa.gov, and if it’s your first time doing that – congratulations! Note that new users will need to create an account, and they’ll guide you to login.gov for that purpose. Don’t fret, it’s very useful to have this account for multiple reasons.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions

If you log in to check on your Social Security account when you’re still young, you’ll see some confusing stuff – basically it tells you how much your payout will be if you continue working and contributing for a ridiculously long 35 year period!Your benefit is calculated by taking an average of your 35 highest years of earnings, which sounds bleak for people like me who only worked a ten-year career, because in theory that average might contain mostly zeroes. But never fear because:

To illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35.  Look at the difference in their benefits:

So the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the big earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI

Even though this has become a long article, it is still far from a complete analysis of the Social Security program. If you want to learn more, I’ve found the AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude, Google Gemini or OpenAI’s Chat GPT) to be shockingly useful at answering questions and running analyses. If you haven’t started using these in your financial research, I highly recommend them. Just search for any of those names (or install the phone app), start typing your questions, and you’ll be learning at a rapid pace within moments.

I get the math, but I didn’t go through your details. The first fundamental question most ask is “when do I take SS? Something that really helped me with the mental math of Social Security is the concept of bend points.

Bend points are lifetime earnings milestones that govern how much Social Security pays out to you. For all income up to the first bend point, you get about 90 cents back from Social Security for every dollar you pay in. After that, it drops off steeply. For income between the first and second bend points, you get more like 32 cents on the dollar, and after the second bend point, you get about 15 cents.

Right now in 2026, you hit the first bend point at something like $540,000 of total lifetime earnings, and the second bend point is around $3.25 million.

The great news for early retirees is that, because Social Security’s payout formula tails off so quickly for higher earners (as you mentioned in the article), it really doesn’t matter very much that we won’t have 35 full years of contributions. Just by working a few years, we get most of the benefits. After that, it’s a game of diminishing returns where you have to work for years and years just to increase your benefit by a small amount. No thanks – I’d rather be retired!

Social security Whoa Nellie! Yes, of course you can start taking SS at age 62. As mentioned above, if you have taxable income above about $22,000, then $1 of SS is withheld per $2 of earnings above the $22,000. Not to worry, when you reach your full retirement age, you get the withheld money back. But those withheld dollars can’t be invested from age 62-67. Next, you can’t just “toss your SS check into an index fund and make 6% after inflation.” First, those capital gains might be taxed at 0, 15, or even 20%. More importantly, those are not guaranteed. Social security goes up 8% per year of delayed filing, PLUS inflation. And those increases, unlike the aforementioned index funds, are not subject to taxation along the way. So filing early and index funding vs delayed filing is comparing a speculative taxable strategy with a guaranteed tax deferred strategy.

It’s not taxable income that counts towards the $22,000, it is earned income. The two can be quite different (think dividends, interest, capital gains vs. salary).

You can certainly include NPV of SS in your Net Worth Statement. It is an Asset (it has monetary value). An asset doesn’t need to be immediately convertible to cash in order to count as an asset – there are simple examples such as a house (that takes time and has costs associated in turning the asset into ‘money’) and more complicated ones like REITs and annuities. They are all Assets as they have monetary value.

What is probably more logical to do is including SS as a Retirement Asset – or those assets you plan to live off of in retirement. This is often a different list of assets than what is in your Net Worth Statement – and is used for a different purpose (creating a stream of cash to live off of in retirement).

I’ve always questioned the “better to wait to withdraw for maximum benefits” position. That may be true for non-mustachians who need every dollar of SS to live on and are willing to work longer to maximize their annual income. But SS’s early and delayed adjustments are actuarially derived to ensure the total cost to the system is the same. Theoretically, you would receive the same amount over your lifetime. Claiming earlier is a hedge against dying young. Unless you have a crystal ball and are assured of living longer than average, it’s better to claim early and invest. I looked into this a few years ago, and came across the paper: https://crr.bc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/IB_19-18.pdf

It’s a great summary of the history of delayed and early options (early claiming was originally designed to allow the younger spouse to not be penalized for retiring with the older spouse). It also analyzes whether the assumptions for the original actuarial adjustments apply today. Summary: adjustments for taking early (65) are probably right. It’s a wash to take anytime after 65. However, higher earners live longer and delay more. If delayed adjustments were based on those who actually use it, the increase should be less. Based on increased life expectancies, wealthier individuals should wait.

I want to call out a couple considerations around the longevity of Social Security and Medicare for those in the USA.

First, there is a provision within the Social Security legislation that stipulates should Social Security funding be deficient to pay out all intended benefits, it will still pay out based on its annual tax intake. While the Social Security funding is quickly dwindling, the expectation is that the annual tax intake will continue to represent ~80% of intended benefits. Thus, even if you don’t expect Congress to actively fix Social Security funding, unless you expect Congress to actively kill Social Security then you should expect some payout.

That said, it is important to note that Medicare has no such deficiency stipulation in its legislation, so if Medicare funding becomes deficient then without an active effort from Congress it will just be gone. I know that early retirees typically plan for medical coverage between retirement and becoming Medicare eligible, but I’ve seen many assume Medicare will be there, which it may not. On one hand, ACA coverage creates a cost-capped option at age 65+, but that assumes that ACA coverage is still around. I know MMM has also suggested options such as self-funding or community plans, but I’ll warn that those are generally more viable for those early retirement years and become generally less viable for many as you get into your golden years. This is where HSAs can be really helpful, and since they can double up as 401k-like funds for non-medical expenses after 65, I really do recommend taking advantage of them as best as you can. Everyone’s costs and longevity will vary, and potentially significantly so if you require long-term care, but there is a general rule of thumb of trying to have ~$200k/person at age 65 bucketed for retirement medical expenses (premiums and out-of-pocket costs), where the expectation is that bucket should continue to grow despite withdrawals in the early years and then transition to mostly drawing down as you get further up in the years.

After all – if we’re going to neglect risk, why not use Berkshire Hathaway’s historical return of 20% per year? Or Bitcoin’s of 230% per year?

Using the proper 2% instead of 6% would lead us to the opposite conclusion as this article. That is, claiming at 62 is the WORST choice if you’ll live until 90.

I realize this might torpedo the entire article. But it’ll also lead the audience to reach better retirement conclusions.

I’m excited to see this topic! Most people I ask (including financial advisors and moneywise folks) insist that it’s almost always better to defer drawing Social Security until normal retirement age (67) or even later (70). However, most people don’t understand the time value of money! I retired four years ago at age 57 and I’m very much looking forward to drawing Social Security next year at age 62. Why? Because it’s a much, much better deal. Here’ s how it works. Using the data provided to me by the Social Security Administration, my current estimated monthly benefit amounts will be $2,513 if starting at age 62, or $3,569 if starting at age 67, and $4,425 if starting at age 70. It appears obvious that it would be best to wait for the higher amount. But it is not. Here’s why. In a zero-interest rate world, I can run a simple break-even analysis and determine that it would take me until age 78½ to come out ahead by waiting until 67 to start. It would take me until age 80½ to break even if I waited until 70 to start. With a current life expectancy for me to live until age 76½, I’m still better off to start at age 62, but only slightly. But then again, we don’t live in a zero-interest rate world! In a 4% interest rate world, these figures change dramatically. It now takes me until age 85½ to break even when starting at age 67, and until age 87 when starting at age 70. In an 8% interest rate world (The S&P 500 has averaged 10.5% annually since 1957), my break-even points are both now out beyond 100 years old. It’s really a no-brainer!

Hey Pete, Regarding your comment on you won’t care about the taxes on your RMDs when you’re 75 because you’ll have plenty of income. I take issue with that as a 75 year old with a six figure retirement income living a comfy life in expensive Boulder County like you. I don’t want to pay taxes to a federal government that is spending in areas that are not my values. But that’s not my main point. Only a couple people have commented on SS taxability (e.g., Jiri, Dave) aside from taxes on RMDs. Not everyone realizes that up to 85% of your SS income is taxable depending on what other kinds of annual retirement income you have. The IRS uses a formula where tax-deferred pensions, royalties, 401K distributions, and any earned income can trigger the taxability of your SS payment. The way to potentially avoid this with the present laws is to pay taxes on any future funds when you’re working, i.e., Roth contributions, Roth conversions, and backdoor Roths if you’re over the Roth eligibility limits. This works best for 1099 people, but W-2 people also can benefit from it to a lesser extent. I’m a believer it’s not how much you make, but how much you keep from the government.

However, if you are a high earner in your working years, it makes sense to max the traditional retirements accounts to avoid a (currently) 24% or 32% tax rate (which was actually quite a bit higher in the past), not worry as much about Roth, and then pay the tax on Social Security. Odds are that the tax on your Social Security will fall in the 12% bracket, or maybe 22% if you are making particularly substantial withdrawals from traditional retirement accounts.

#8420. Original Medicare Has No Out-of-Pocket Limit – Add One Before You Need Care

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Original Medicare puts no yearly limit on your out-of-pocket costs. Cap them with a Medigap policy like Plan G or a Medicare Advantage plan. If you choose Medigap, buy it in your six-month open enrollment window, when insurers can’t turn you down or charge more for your health.

Millions go without either one. KFF found that in 2023, 3.5 million people, 13% of everyone in traditional Medicare, lacked any supplemental coverage.

Without it, your share of Part B care is usually 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the $283 deductible. By our math, a $100,000 year of outpatient cancer treatment leaves you more than $20,000 to pay. Part A adds a $1,736 hospital deductible in 2026 that you can owe more than once a year, plus daily charges for long hospital and skilled nursing stays.

Your Medigap window opens the first month you’re 65 or older with Part B, and it never repeats. Outside it, insurers in most states can ask health questions, then turn you down or charge more, unless a guaranteed issue right applies, such as your Advantage plan pulling out of your area.

To price Medigap, start with Mutual of Omaha. AM Best rates Mutual of Omaha Insurance Company A+ (Superior). Its online tool quotes Plan G and High-Deductible Plan G from your ZIP code, birth date, and sex, without asking for contact details. On Sept. 23, 2026, it quoted High-Deductible Plan G at $45.84 to $52.19 a month for a 65-year-old woman in Dallas (75201), Columbus (43215), and Phoenix (85004). Couples can save with its household discount where it’s available, though the amount and rules vary by state.

Plan G covers the same benefits at every insurer, so compare your Mutual of Omaha quote with Medicare.gov’s list for your ZIP code before you apply.

#8419. Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

Donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident. Already outdoorsy, he graduated from long hikes to planning to climb all 53 of Colorado’s 14,000’ers (mountains above 14,000 feet, or 4,267m). While researching which peaks required overnight camping, he realized that some people’s hikes just keep going.

“I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada. That’s just ridiculous,” Rice explained. “I fell in love with that idea.”

From there, it was a slippery slope. First came the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), from the Mexican border in California to the Canadian border in British Columbia. Then he did the Continental Divide Trail (CDT), tracing the Rocky Mountains from New Mexico to the Montana-Canada border. Before he knew it, he had a trail name — Iceman —and was working the gig economy to free up time for wilderness adventures.

But that’s where most people’s slippery slope levels out. Hiking the 4,988km CDT is as meaty a project as most of us can imagine. But for Rice, it only opened the floodgates. He was fascinated by everything that didn’t make it into famous routes, especially the ridges and mountains he passed in his home state of Colorado that were just off trail.

“There’s all this stuff the CDT doesn’t hit because it is following the Continental Divide,” he told ExplorersWeb. “So when I got to the end of the Colorado section, about 700 miles, I was thinking, man, if there were a 2,000-mile version of that, it would be my dream thru-hike. Just that non-stop, relentless brutality that is Colorado.”

Colorado has 14,000′ peaks but also deserts. Photo: Donovan Rice

Rice started thinking about a massive thru-hike loop of the state. His idea was to stitch together existing trails and form new ones where necessary.

“I dropped a load of pins across the areas in Colorado I wanted to visit, then I pulled out a public lands layer of the map to see how I might connect the areas,” he explained. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness. I wanted to see beautiful views, I wanted to cover as much of Colorado’s diversity as possible, and I wanted to take the most iconic and epic route possible.”

Unlike places like the UK, there is no “right to roam” in Colorado, so connecting the route to avoid private land was tricky. Occasionally, he had to link bits of public land and sections of trail in the “least worst way,” with short road walks when private property appeared to halt progress.

As he tacked on mountain peaks and the national parks he wanted to explore, his route swelled to a monstrous 3,000km+. His itinerary now included all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, three of its national parks, 13 14,000’ers and 47 13,000’ers.

“This is not an efficient route,” Rice admits. “You could walk the full perimeter of Colorado and then hike the Colorado Trail [an existing 885km trail from Waterton Canyon near Denver to Durango], and then still have kilometers left over [to complete the loop].”

The Great Colorado Route. Photo: Donovan Rice

The route looked epic on paper, but Rice still needed to prove it could actually be thru-hiked. After months of planning, Rice set off on his Great Colorado Route from Gunnison National Park on May 14, 2026. He traveled ultra-light, carrying just six kilos of gear, with just a quilt instead of a sleeping bag and a tarp rather than a tent.

“I wanted it to be lightweight enough that I could be nimble on the mountains while doing these technical traverses,” said Rice. Traveling light was wise. Rice’s Great Colorado Route is challenging, with plenty of scrambling and sustained time at altitude.

“The crux might be between Bailey and Rocky Mountain National Park. You go over the Mount Evans Wilderness, two 14,000’ers, hop on the Front Range across several 13,000’ers, and then across the Tenmile Range, and then the absolutely brutal Gore Range.”

Rice spent 141 days tramping his trail, eventually finishing on October 1 after 3,252km. While he describes the route as “definitely not beginner-friendly” — due to plenty of cross-country terrain, off-trail navigation, and route-finding — it doesn’t require mountaineering skills.

“For me, the real sweet spot is Class three scrambling,” he says. “Once you get up to Class four, it starts getting really scary, and I had no tolerance at all for true Class five rock climbing.”

However, he did pack an ice ax, micro-spikes, snow gaiters, and a lightweight helmet to protect against rockfall. He also made an effort to structure the route to provide relief between the most challenging sections, giving the trail an ebb and flow, and potential hikers time to decompress.

The Ballard to La Junta traverse. Photo: Donovan Rice

Overall, his focus on scenic beauty over contrived difficulty helped keep the route somewhat accessible. This is important because Rice hopes that other hikers will give it a go. He is building a website that maps the route, segment by segment, with GPS coordinates to help future hikers find the best places to camp or alternative paths depending on trail conditions. This is a May-through-October trail, but Rice stresses that it is unrealistic to expect perfect conditions for four and a half months.

“This is one of those routes where bailouts will have to happen,” Rice explained. “You’ll have to take a low route or an alternate. I’m hoping to revisit some of the areas in the future and establish some of these alternative routes.”

He aims to get all 29 segments of the initial route fully mapped on The Great Colorado website by the end of the year. It’s a big project, almost as big as the hike itself.

“I need to see how many people will actually give it a try. People can do segments. I’d love to see more thru-hikers do this, but the big challenge is that I think the majority of thru-hikers will look at this and think ‘that’s above my pay grade’.”

The Castles, Colorado. Photo: Donovan Rice

Once he finishes the website, the level of interest might dictate his next steps. “I don’t know what level of formal recognition I want to try for. Do I want to try to get it codified? Or should it stay unofficial and remain just some cool thing someone did that published information on how to do it yourself.”

Whether or not his Great Colorado Route ever gains the name recognition of the CDT or PCT, Rice has authored something unique, and in a world full of rehashes and copycats, that makes it special.

#8418. Higher Deductibles Cut Auto & Home Premiums – If Your Emergency Fund Can Cover Them

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Raising your auto and homeowners deductibles cuts your premiums every year, but it only works if you could pay the higher amount tomorrow without borrowing. Get a quote at a $1,000 deductible on each policy, and make the switch only if your emergency fund could cover both deductibles at once.

The Insurance Information Institute estimates that raising a car’s collision and comprehensive deductible from $200 to $500 can cut the cost of that coverage by 15% to 30%. Going from $200 to $1,000 can cut that cost by 40% or more. On a homeowners policy, raising the deductible from $500 to $1,000 can cut the premium by as much as 25%.

The catch is timing. You collect the savings a little at a time, every year you don’t file a claim, and you pay the higher deductible all at once on every claim you do file. Say moving from $500 to $1,000 saves $125 a year. It takes four claim-free years for the savings to cover the extra $500 out of pocket.

That’s why your emergency fund decides it. One hailstorm can dent your car and your roof on the same afternoon, and that’s two deductibles due at once. Some homeowners policies also carry a separate wind or hail deductible, usually 1% to 5% of the home’s insured value, that stays in place whatever you pick for the standard one.

If you couldn’t pay the higher deductible this week without a credit card, keep the lower one until your savings catch up.

#8417. Bodies of Missing Japanese Climbers Found on Gangapurna West

This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West.

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the 7,140m mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

A search-and-rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

The team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

#8415. Introducing the Banff Mountain Book Competition Winners, 2026

Every year, the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival celebrates the best mountain and adventure writing, film, and photography. The literary highlight of this alpine-themed celebration is the Banff Mountain Book Competition, with eight categories and one grand prize. The jury will award the grand prize at the festival, but the category winners have been announced.

First, the two Special Jury Mentions. Jack Plant’s Spirit of the Great Bear showcases his spectacular photography of the Great Bear Forest. Meanwhile, Ian Nicholson’s Glacier Travel & Crevasse Rescue: Essential Skills for Snow Travel does exactly what it says on the tin. “Of all the skill sets required for mountain climbing, perhaps none are as intimidating as glacier travel. But with carefully crafted instructions and illustrations, Nicholson takes us behind the curtain,” jury member Lauren DeLaunay Miller explains.

The Mountain Literature award went to Lone Wolf: Walking the Line Between Civilization and Wildness by Adam Weymouth. Weymouth dives into the place of wild animals in modern Europe, a continent “undergoing profound climatic, environmental, and political changes.”

Black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival by Trina Moyles won the Environmental Literature category. “Black Bear seamlessly weaves together two complex storylines, laying bare Moyles’ relationships with her brother and with the wildlife she meets while working in a fire watch tower in Alberta.”

The Mountain Article prize, awarded to a magazine piece rather than a book, went to The Misfits by Chad Heddleston. Heddleston chose to profile rock climbing couple Jan and Herb Conn. “These two exist in the spirit and austerity of the pioneering European climbers of the early 20th century. The writing highlights their uniqueness and the integrity of their life choices,” jury member David Chambre said.

Pioneering rock climbers Jan and Herb Conn. Photo: Dwight Deal

The Adventure Travel prize went to North to the Future: An Offline Adventure through the Changing Wilds of Alaska by Ben Weissenbach. “Weissenbach — an L.A. native with little prior wilderness experience — treks through the Alaskan tundra with a series of eccentric environmental scientists and returns with a new perspective on technology and a revitalized sense of wonder for the natural world.”

Cabin Wild: Alpine Bivouac Huts by Ben Tibbetts won the Guidebook award. “A captivating volume that invites us to see the Alps in a new light, through an intimate journey around a selection of bivouac huts across Italy, Switzerland, and France,” according to jury member Rob Lovell.

The Mountain Image award went to Fjell: A Faithful Witness by Orsolya Haarberg. “A highly original book that takes us on a journey through the Norwegian highlands. It is as much an art book as a book about mountains,” explains jury member David Chambre.

Finally, The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland by Guy Robertson & Hamish Frost won the Climbing Literature prize. “The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland combines stunning photography and evocative essays in a truly spectacular ode to Scottish winter climbing. By profiling important routes through the eyes of the climbers who created them, Guy Robertson and Hamish Frost have created an exceptional book.”

The category-winning authors get cash prizes and a chance to win the grand prize at the festival on November 5.

#8413. The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

For nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it showed Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

In the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first important Italian treatise on the subject.

Vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

Sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:

“The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”

Vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library

Sella’s most important Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

Muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

The peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

Muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella

Sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

From other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

Muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

The British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

The French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

The British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

From there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

On July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

Muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours

The French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance quickly showed the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

They fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

After the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

The British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

The two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

Far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

The southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal

Since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

In August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal

Four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a new route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

The 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

Muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal

Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8412. Ignore Wrong-Number Texts – Many Crypto Investment Scams Start With a Reply

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A friendly text meant for someone else is a common opening for crypto investment scams, and a polite reply is exactly what the scammer wants. Don’t answer, even to say it’s the wrong number. If someone you met by text ever brings up investing, stop replying and never invest where they tell you to.

Picture a text from an unknown number that reads, “Hi Jessica, I confirmed our dinner reservation for Friday at 7!” Pointing out the mistake feels like simple courtesy, but to a scammer, your reply proves a friendly person is on the other end.

The FBI and the Federal Trade Commission describe what comes next. The stranger apologizes and keeps the chat going until it becomes a friendship or a romance. Then they mention how well they’re doing trading crypto and offer to show you how. Early on, the trading site they steer you to shows fast gains and often lets you withdraw some, which makes it look real. When you try to cash out everything, the account freezes and the site says you owe “taxes” or fees to unlock it.

Crypto investment fraud was the biggest source of losses reported to the FBI in 2025, at $7.2 billion. When the FBI contacted 3,780 victims that year to warn them, 78% didn’t know they were being scammed.

Instead of replying, forward the text to 7726 (SPAM), which helps your carrier block similar messages, then delete it.

If you’ve already replied, these signs give the scam away:

How long you’ve been talking doesn’t matter. Never put money into an investment that someone you met online introduced.

If you’ve already sent money, stop. Don’t pay a tax or release fee to free your balance, since paying never unlocks it. Report the scam at ic3.gov, the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, with every transaction detail you have.

Then expect a second scam. The FBI says almost every victim later hears from a fake lawyer, recovery firm, or law enforcement officer who offers to get the money back for a fee. The FBI never asks victims for money, so treat any recovery offer that comes with a fee as the next scam.

#8411. Weekend Warm-Up: First Descent Rio Cuervo

This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.

With an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it. Dane Jackson launches into the complicated business of trip logistics, trying to find a way to get the team and their equipment to the beginning of the river. Besides him, the team consists of the trip’s mastermind, Kilian Astorga, and kayakers Tom Dolle, Eirik Hansen, Adrian Mattern, and David Sodomka.

Forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows. It’s gone now, so they turn to helicopter transport. With their gear dangling below on a rope, the chopper carries them up into the mountain, depositing kayaks and kayakers alike on the lakeshore. They set up camp and settle in to begin the first descent of the Rio Cuervo.

The team scouts the head of the river, swelled with recent rainfall. Photo: Screenshot

The dense forest and sometimes steep banks add another layer of difficulty as they begin to make their way downstream. They have to plan ahead, as there are stretches where it is impossible to bail if the rapids become too much. This means more portaging, which is painfully slow due to the thick vegetation.

When they do hit the rapids, on-board cameras capture the frenetic energy of whitewater kayaking. But the film makes no attempt to conceal the reality of a first descent. Much of their time is spent scouting ahead by drone, poring over satellite images, portaging, and standing about debating logistics.

Sunset arrives before the end of their portage. Camping in the jungle makes for an uncomfortable night. Photo: Screenshot

Jackson and the rest of the crew soldier on, though, cracking nerdy jokes (the jungle is compared to both Dagobah and Fangorn Forest) and making the best of bad weather and rough camping. In the final few days, conditions improve, and they can spend more time on the water.

The contrast between their slow, grueling push forward and the wild speed on the river brings refreshing energy to the kayaking sections. When the river finally widens as they glide into the sea, it feels like a hard-won victory.

Early in the production of a certain musical, Broadway director Harold Prince attempted to ask Andrew Lloyd Weber what the deeper political allegory or social commentary was behind the composer’s feline opus. Weber famously took a long pause and replied: “Hal, this is just about cats.”

This movie is about kayaking. Many outdoor adventure films use the genre, and the adventure story, to explore grand themes, and some do so successfully. But when they fall flat, is it more annoying than I can begin to express. For that reason, I deeply respect the clarity of purpose evinced by Dan Jackson and First Descent Rio Cuervo.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8409. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Lara Neumeier Makes First Female Ascent of a 5.14c: On October 7, Lara Neumeier made the first female ascent of Rhapsody (E11 7a/5.14c) at Dumbarton Rock, Scotland. She succeeded 20 years after Dave MacLeod established the route as the world’s first E11.

Neumeier’s ascent makes her the fifth woman to climb a 5.14c trad route. In an interview, she discussed the 15 climbing days and two visits spent working the route, how it compares to other routes, and her hope that the ascent will encourage more women to attempt the iconic line.

Karl Bushby, shortly after starting and now. Photo Facebook

I Left My 8-Year-Old Son Behind 28 Years Ago to Walk Around the World: After 28 years walking around the world, Karl Bushby should complete this Goliath Expedition within the next month. Now he faces an emotional homecoming: his son, whom he left behind at the age of eight, is now 36. Bushby has a grandchild he has never met, and his mother has seen him only three times since he left.

Julia Clarke hikes beside a stream in Mull, Scotland. Photo: Julia Clarke

Here are Nine British Hiking Rules Americans Need to Know: After returning to Scotland after more than a decade in Colorado, Julia Clarke realized she needed to rethink her mountain skills. She warns Americans not to underestimate the weather, terrain, or seemingly puny hills in Britain.

From wild camping rules and differences in hiking trails, to avoiding cows and brushing up on your navigational skills, she shares nine key differences American hikers should understand before tackling the British backcountry.

Women Across Diving Speak Out on Harassment: Women across the diving industry are speaking out about sexual harassment and assault. After years of raising concerns, petitioning and reporting to expedition operators and dive agencies with little outcome, many are taking to social media to share the experiences that have affected their careers as instructors, expedition leaders, and marine professionals.

Campaigners are demanding that the industry establish better and more accessible reporting systems, better safeguarding standards, and that operators vet their staff properly.

The Art of Progress: Climbing ethics are constantly evolving, and many are now reconsidering whether traditional ground-up ascents, minimal bolting, and preserving the original character of a route should take precedence over safety, accessibility, and the experience of future climbers.

Derek Franz explores this debate by looking at lines across Yosemite, Madagascar, Germany, and Patagonia, and the work underway to replace corroded bolts in many of them. The approach challenges the idea that a first ascent should remain untouched.

Three Dead After Avalanche in Chile: On October 17, an avalanche swept seven mountaineers into Laguna del Inca near Chile’s Ski Portillo resort. Three were killed and four injured.

The group was climbing toward Cerro Los Tres Hermanos when they triggered a slab avalanche. Rescue teams and the police responded within 10 minutes, and the survivors were airlifted to hospital. According to resort management, the group had entered a restricted area marked as an avalanche danger zone despite earlier warnings.

Old Traditions and New Developments on Mt. Kenya: Giovanni Trambaiolo explores Mount Kenya’s climbing history, especially the overlooked contributions of Kenyan climbers and the mountain’s deep spiritual significance to indigenous communities. He describes opening up Rainmaker, the new six-pitch trad route on the Temple Cliffs of Mount Kenya.

Three Mountain Emergencies in 14 Hours: Three hunting emergencies in northwest Colorado prompted search-and-rescue crews to respond within 14 hours, as the first significant snowfall of the season coincided with the opening of elk season on October 14 and 15.

Their first rescue call was for an overdue hunter, and the second from an individual who became separated from their group near Bears Ears and was too cold to walk. A third hunter suffered serious injuries when a tree fell on their tent as they slept. Another hunting party did not require rescue but got caught in snow, mud, and fog and spent over four hours finding their way back to camp.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8407. Beware, A Disability Can Force You Into Early Retirement

Earlier this year, I was sick for two weeks. Unfortunately, I’ve had asthma since I was a kid. So when a respiratory illness hits, I tend to cough and suffer longer than the average person.

During COVID, my asthma flared up more often, likely due to the stress of having a baby during a pandemic.

It’s the type of breathing where you’re annoyingly conscious of every breath. You can never quite fill your lungs to 100%. In my case, it felt more like 75%.

On Wednesday, August 12, still sick, I decided to keep a previously scheduled consulting call with an FS reader. I had booked it assuming I’d be better by then. I wasn’t.

By the end of our 1 hour, 15 minute session, where I spent about 80% of the time talking, I was wiped out. My energy had dropped to maybe 30%. When you’re talking nonstop, you’re not breathing deeply or regularly. I felt like I was slowly suffocating while discussing their asset allocation.

The call reminded me of the many days I felt physically drained talking to clients during my 13 years in finance. As my responsibilities and stress grew, I eventually hit a breaking point. I’d rather earn nothing and be free and healthy than keep grinding myself down.

Just the other day, I couldn’t bend down to pick something up without a sharp pain shooting through my spine. I almost collapsed.

The last time I felt pain this bad was in 2023. I had spent an hour sitting on the ground signing copies of Buy This Not That for readers who donated to victims of the Maui fires. My dad is from Hawaii, and seeing thousands of lives upended overnight weighed on me. The Financial Samurai community ended up donating about $48,000. But when the signing was over, I couldn’t stand up and I called my wife for help.

My theory is that these episodes are triggered by a combination of prolonged stress and me forgetting I’m not 25 anymore.

This time, I clearly forgot. On Sunday, I played two hours of 4.5-level pickleball, then taught my kids for another hour. On Monday, I played 1.5 hours of intense tennis with plenty of serving. Then on Tuesday, several dads in our dad bod challenge shared their gym Personal Records, so naturally I went for personal records too. Instead of my usual three sets of 10-12 reps, I did five sets with progressive loading.

Wednesday morning, my back was already grumbling. So of course I went on a hilly 30-minute walk at 7:05am before breakfast and the school drop off. Walking downhill to school, the pain returned. By the time I got home, I could no longer walk normally.

If I still had a day job, there’s no way I could have gone into the office. And if my asthma flared up at the same time, I couldn’t speak to clients for more than an hour or two a day.

Not being able to provide for my family would be a terrible thing.

These two episodes forced me to confront a few uncomfortable truths:

Some people picture disability as a dramatic car accident or a fall off a ladder. Reality is far more boring. Accidental injuries make up only about 9% to 12% of long-term disability claims, while musculoskeletal problems like back and joint pain are the leading cause, at 26% to 33% of claims.

According to the Social Security Administration (SSA), roughly one in four 20-year-olds will be out of work for at least a year because of a disabling condition before reaching normal retirement age. That’s one quarter of all 20-year-olds, not just those in high-risk occupations.

In other words, the thing that takes you out of the workforce probably won’t be a skydiving mishap. It’ll be your back after one too many weightlifting attempts.

Before getting into what to do, it’s worth understanding the two main types of disability coverage. They work very differently.

Short-term disability (STD) covers you for a temporary inability to work, like recovering from surgery, a bad back, or a serious illness. Benefits typically replace around 50% to 70% of your income and last anywhere from a few weeks to about six months. The waiting period, called the elimination period, is usually short, often one to two weeks.

Many employers provide short-term disability as a benefit. A handful of states also run their own programs, including California (SDI), New York, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Hawaii (TDI). If you’re self-employed, you probably have nothing unless you bought it yourself.

Long-term disability (LTD) kicks in when a disability lasts longer, usually after a 90-day elimination period. It typically replaces about 60% of your income and can pay for a set number of years or until age 65. This is the coverage that actually protects your family’s financial future. Short-term disability is a speed bump. Long-term disability is a car crash.

And no, don’t count on Social Security Disability Insurance to save you. SSDI is hard to qualify for, has a five-month waiting period, and the monthly benefit is modest. It’s a floor, not a plan.

If you have a job with benefits, log into your HR portal today and look at your LTD coverage. Many group policies cap monthly benefits, which means high earners may only be replacing a fraction of their income.

If there’s a gap, buy a supplemental individual policy, ideally with an own-occupation rider. It’s portable, so it stays with you if you leave your job. If you’re self-employed like me, individual LTD is the only coverage you’ll have. Get quotes while you’re young and healthy, because pre-existing conditions get excluded or priced up later.

Even with great coverage, there’s a gap. Short-term disability might make you wait a week or two, and long-term disability usually makes you wait 90 days. Meanwhile, your mortgage, tuition, and Costco runs don’t pause.

Keep at least six months of living expenses in cash or Treasury bills. If you have kids, a single income household, or are self-employed, aim for 12 months. If you’re wondering where the line is between prudent and paranoid, here’s my take on how much savings is too much. The emergency fund is your bridge from healthy to covered.

A single income stream is a single point of failure. If that engine stalls, the whole plane goes down. Your goal is to build a jet with at least four engines, so you can lose one and still land safely.

The best time to start a side hustle is while you still have a steady paycheck and good health. You get to experiment without pressure, and if it fails, you still eat.

I started Financial Samurai in July 2009 while working full-time in finance. I’d wake up early and write before work, then publish again on weekends. For three years, it made very little money. But by the time I left Corporate America in 2012, the site had become a real second engine alongside about $80,000 a year in passive investment income.

Without that second engine, I never would have had the courage to negotiate my way out.

Here’s the key for disability planning: prioritize side hustles that don’t require your body to show up. Driving for Uber or coaching tennis stops the moment your back gives out. Writing, a blog, a YouTube channel, an online course, or a self-published ebook can keep paying while you’re flat on your back.

If you need ideas, my wife put together a list of the 20 best side hustle ideas to make extra money. If you want to go the online route, here’s how to start a blog and build your own platform. I’m biased, but owning your own corner of the internet is the gift that keeps on giving.

One engine is a job. Two engines is a cushion. Four or more engines is freedom.

Your peak earning years are also, conveniently, your peak health years. Don’t assume your income will keep climbing forever. Assume it could drop to zero tomorrow, then save as if that’s true.

Related: Achieving FI With A Visual Impairment

I saved over 50% of my after-tax income starting with my first job out of college because I knew I couldn’t last a lifetime working 70+ hours a week. I didn’t know my lungs and back would eventually join the protest, but the logic held up.

Front-load your savings. Max out your 401(k) and IRA, and invest the excess in a taxable brokerage account. Pay down high fixed costs where you can.

The lower your required monthly expenses, the less income replacement you need if disaster strikes. A paid-off house is one of the best disability insurance policy nobody talks about.

Your ability to earn over the next 20 to 30 years is likely worth millions. Yet we manage our portfolios more carefully than our bodies.

Get annual checkups. But lock down a life insurance policy before you see a doctor for something more. Manage your stress before it manages you. Warm up, cool down, and stop trying to beat the other dads’ PRs after a weekend of nonstop racquet sports. Ask me how I know.

While you’re at it, get your paperwork in order. A will, a durable power of attorney, and a healthcare directive are the basics. But if anyone depends on your income, term life insurance is the most important piece. A disability takes away your ability to earn for a while. Death takes it away for good.

The irony is that the health problems that make you worry about disability also make life insurance more expensive, or harder to get. Lock in coverage while you’re still healthy enough to qualify. I’d compare term life quotes on Policygenius, which lets you see prices from multiple top insurers in one place.

The scary thing about disability is that it rarely announces itself. One day you’re serving aces and going for gym PRs. The next, you can’t walk your kids to school.

Being unable to breathe normally or walk for a few days made me realize how fragile everything is. If you’re the provider for your family, that fragility is your responsibility to plan for.

So check your disability coverage this week. Build your cash buffer. Start a side hustle that doesn’t depend on your body showing up. And for goodness sake, stretch.

Have you ever been unable to work for an extended period due to an illness or injury? Do you know whether your employer’s long-term disability policy is own-occupation or any-occupation, and when it switches? How many engines of income do you have today, and which would keep running if you couldn’t get out of bed? Have you bought supplemental disability insurance, or do you think it’s a waste of money? And what side hustle would you start if your main income disappeared tomorrow?

To get new posts in your inbox as soon as they’re published, ad-free for the first few hours, sign up for the free Financial Samurai newsletter here. Join 60,000+ readers building wealth and breaking free sooner.

This post is about how quickly your ability to earn can disappear. The best defense is building wealth and multiple income streams during your healthiest years, before your back and lungs start filing complaints.

That’s exactly what I lay out in my USA Today bestseller, Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures. I’ve distilled 30 years of experience studying, working in, and writing about personal finance into a roadmap for reaching $1 million and beyond, while you still have the energy to enjoy it.

Get a copy today. Your future self, possibly lying flat on the floor with a bad back, will thank you.

I had a concussion which another cyclist collided into me over a decade ago. I was 54 yrs. I had to learn to walk slowly in lst few wks., I was dizzy just standing in the shower or in front of my kitchen sink, turning. I had to rest for many hours in bed for well over a month. If I walked too fast, I got dizzy from seeing blur of colours of scenery around me, etc. Thankfully as part of employer’s benefit, I had short-term disability insurance which I had to tap into long-term disability insurance. I returned to work lst part-time after 5 months on disability /medical leave. I returned to cycling slowly at 6 months. My partner did all the housework, cooking and food shopping during my recovery. It took me another few additional months to become comfortable even having other cyclists cycle around me.

It scared the beejesus out of me, because I solo paying off my home mortgage. My partner was still paying off his. Sam, this article really hit home for me. At age 55, I began experiencing symptoms of an extremely rare disease. After years of uncertainty, dozens of doctors, and losing nearly 40 pounds, I suffered a stroke at 57 that abruptly ended my career in construction management and real estate development. Fortunately, the stroke spared my speech, cognition, and memory, but permanently impaired my left-side motor control and sensation. Thirteen years later, chronic pain, spasticity, and mobility limitations remain daily challenges. One lesson I’d emphasize is the importance of good health insurance. Medical bills totaled approximately $675,000 over four years, including $485,000 leading up to and including the stroke. Even with insurance, some rehabilitation required appeals or out-of-pocket payments. My stroke also forced me to sell my interest in our development business to my longtime partner. Although we had planned for a buyout in the event of death, disability was a different matter, and we ultimately negotiated an amicable agreement. I was fortunate to have accumulated substantial savings and investments before becoming disabled. Equally important, I was blessed with supportive family and friends, including a sister who’s a professional financial advisor, a physician brother-in-law, a daughter who’s an ER nurse, and a son who’s a mental health therapist. Unable to return to work, I focused more on managing our investments. With my sister’s guidance, we maintained a buy-and-hold approach through major market downturns. I’m a testament to time in the market, not timing the market, and the power of compounding. Our net worth has more than tripled since before the stroke. Meanwhile, rehabilitation remains a lifelong project. Now 71, I recently returned to my longtime neurological physical therapist after a three-year break. I’m still looking for ways to improve my independence, mobility, and quality of life. Forced retirement at 57 certainly didn’t mean the end of a productive and purposeful life. Financial independence can’t restore your health, but it provides options when life changes unexpectedly. My advice: Save and invest early, maintain good insurance, appreciate your support network, and don’t postpone enjoying life while you’re healthy.

Thank you for sharing your experience. It really hits Home, the importance of good health, good health insurance, and spending more intentionally with our one and only lives.

I wish you good health and prosperity. Don’t be a stranger!
